# Baselines, datasets and the fair-comparison protocol {#sec-baselines}

**ISLA is measured against the two public slice-attention transformers
with the strongest record on industrial aerodynamics, GeoTransolver and
Transolver, on three datasets, under one protocol that fixes everything
except the architecture.** The baselines are strong, not straw:
GeoTransolver has at least as many parameters as ISLA and receives raw
coordinates that ISLA never sees; both run at their own best learning rate;
neither is ever modified. This chapter says what each baseline computes and
sees, states one rule about how a problem's global conditions enter any
model, lists the protocol as nine rules, names the datasets and their
splits, and closes with the protocol table every cross-architecture number
in the book is produced under.

```{python}
#| label: setup-baselines
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
```

## The baselines and what each one sees {#sec-part-baseline}

**GeoTransolver and Transolver share ISLA's routing mechanism and differ in
what they are allowed to see: raw coordinates in a frame, and the problem's
global vector as a raw feature.** Transolver (Wu et al., ICML 2024, arXiv
[2402.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02366)) is a transformer for physics
fields on unstructured point sets. Each layer assigns every point a softmax
mixture over a fixed number of *slices*, pools point features into one token
per slice, runs attention among the slice tokens, and scatters the result
back through the same mixture: *physics attention*. GeoTransolver adds a
geometry encoder and a global-context projector. @fig-family-diagram places
ISLA beside them.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-family-diagram
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   What each architecture is handed, and where they differ. Gray boxes
%%|   are data; the routing mechanism (solid blue) is shared by the whole
%%|   family. GeoTransolver and Transolver receive coordinates in the
%%|   dataset's frame and the global vector as a vector; ISLA receives only
%%|   invariants of the same inputs and its slices carry the surface measure
%%|   (dashed blue: fixed maps with no parameters). How to read this: the
%%|   diagram shows inputs and structure, not accuracy; the learned blocks are
%%|   the same kind of object in all three.
flowchart LR
    classDef data fill:#f4f3ee,stroke:#898781,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef learned fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef fixed fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2a78d6,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#0b0b0b

    subgraph B["GeoTransolver / Transolver"]
        direction TB
        B1["per point: centered coordinates, unit normal<br/>global: the far-field vector (a unit direction under the protocol)"]:::data
        B2["GeoTransolver only: geometry encoder,<br/>global-context projector"]:::learned
        B3["physics attention × layers:<br/>softmax routing of points into slices,<br/>attention among slices, scatter back"]:::learned
        B4["linear head: pressure, wall shear"]:::learned
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4
    end
    subgraph I["ISLA"]
        direction TB
        I1["per point: position, unit normal, measure weight<br/>global: unit direction(s), scalars"]:::data
        I2["invariant seed; length unit = RMS pairwise distance"]:::fixed
        I3["slice layers × 12:<br/>measure-weighted routing, anchors,<br/>relational invariants, read-back"]:::learned
        I4["linear head on invariants → equivariant basis"]:::fixed
        I1 --> I2 --> I3 --> I4
    end
```

**GeoTransolver** is the recipe's default surface model. Per surface point
it receives the coordinates, centered on the case, and the unit normal as a
six-channel feature; the far-field vector is a three-channel global feature.
Its *geometry encoder* takes the coordinates a second time through a
dedicated embedding path that conditions the slice attention; the
ball-query local-feature path is off throughout this program, because it is
off in the recipe's shipped configuration; the GeoTransolver compared here
is therefore the one a user gets by running the recipe unmodified, not the
strongest configuration the class can express. It is not rotation- or
translation-equivariant: rotate the car and it sees a different input
(@sec-pose).

::: {#sec-transolver}
**Transolver** is the same family without the geometry encoder, the control
that isolates what the encoder contributes. Per point it receives coordinates
and normal; the far-field vector is broadcast to every point.
:::

**ISLA** receives position, unit normal and measure weight per point and
each global direction as a unit vector, consumed only through invariants
and equivariant anchors (@sec-isla). @tbl-architectures gives the three
configurations side by side; the parameter counts and training footprints
are in @tbl-isla-cost. On the interior tasks the baseline is
GeoTransolver-volume, the recipe's volume configuration of the same class,
described with those tasks in @sec-interior.

| architecture | per-point inputs | global input | layers | hidden | slices |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| GeoTransolver | centered coordinates, unit normal; coordinates again through the geometry encoder | the far-field vector through the global-context projector: a unit direction under the protocol | 12 | 256 | 256 |
| Transolver | centered coordinates, unit normal | the far-field vector, broadcast per point: a unit direction under the protocol | 8 | 256 | 256 |
| ISLA | position, unit normal, measure weight, through invariants and anchors only | unit direction(s) and global scalars | 12 | see @sec-using-config | 256 |

: The three architectures compared on the aerodynamic datasets. *Per-point
inputs*: channels attached to each of the 200,000 sampled surface cells per
case under the reporting protocol. *Layers*: soft-slice attention blocks.
*Hidden*: width of the per-point feature. How to read this: the table
states what each model is handed, not how accurate it is or what it costs
(@sec-using-cost). Configuration source:
`unified_external_aero_recipe/conf/model/{isla_surface,geotransolver_surface,transolver_surface}.yaml`.
{#tbl-architectures}

### Global directions enter as unit vectors, magnitudes as scalars {#sec-unit-direction-rule}

**A problem's global conditions enter every architecture in one form:
directions as unit vectors, magnitudes as scalars.** The rule is a property
of the problem, not of any dataset's units. A direction carries no scale;
whatever scale the pipeline attaches to it (the units the solver ran in) is
an accident of the dataset that a model would have to learn to ignore. A
magnitude that matters physically, a far-field speed or a Reynolds number,
is a separate scalar with its own place in the input. ISLA enforces the
rule by construction: it normalizes its global vectors and takes magnitudes
only through `global_scalars` (@sec-isla-inputs). GeoTransolver and
Transolver consume whatever vector the pipeline hands them, so for them the
rule is a protocol requirement, and every dataset pipeline of the recipe
writes the far-field direction as a unit vector.

The motivating control is visible before training. GeoTransolver's
global-context projector applies linear maps and a slice softmax to the
vector directly, so its conditioning depends on the magnitude. At unit
magnitude a head of the untrained projector spreads over most of the 256
slices; at the magnitude of the HiLiftAeroML solver's velocity (in inches
per second) it routes almost all of its weight to one (@tbl-projector).
Transolver concatenates the raw vector into every point's features, with
the same hazard in a different place. Training can in principle rescale
either path, so these numbers are the initialization signature; the trained
measurement, in the collapsed note below, is what the rule rests on.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-projector
#| output: asis
cond = J("geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json")["results"]
out = "| magnitude of the global vector | occupied slices per head (entropy-equivalent, min to max over heads) | largest context entry |\n|---:|---|---:|\n"
labels = {1.0: "1 (unit direction)", 38.9: "38.9 (DrivAerML's velocity, m/s)", 2679.5054741899685: "2,679.5 (HiLiftAeroML's velocity, in/s)"}
for r in cond:
    lab = next(v for k, v in labels.items() if abs(k - r["drive_magnitude"]) < 1e-6)
    out += f"| {lab} | {r['effective_slices_min']:.1f} to {r['effective_slices_max']:.1f} of 256 | {r['context_abs_max']:.2f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Conditioning of GeoTransolver's global-context projector at initialization against the magnitude of the "
      "global vector it receives, at the recipe's projector dimensions with untrained weights. "
      "How to read this: a head that occupies one slice has lost its ability to condition on the direction; "
      "this is a property of the untrained network, and the trained consequence is in the note below. "
      "Data: results/geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-projector}")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The trained consequence, at the exploration budget"}
At 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases with the same cases, seeds and budget in
both arms, GeoTransolver and Transolver fed the unit direction are each more
accurate than their physical-velocity twin on every one of the 180
validation cases, by a median factor above three (@tbl-unit-vs-physical).
The table is a control on an input scale, measured at the exploration
budget of 10,000 cells; it makes no accuracy claim about any architecture
and appears nowhere else in the book.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-unit-vs-physical
#| output: asis
fp35 = J("fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json")["runs"]
ud = J("udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json")["paired"]
fp = lambda keys: [fp35[k]["fields"]["pressure_l2"]["fp32_mean"] for k in keys]
arms = [
    ("GeoTransolver, physical velocity, lr 1e-3", fp([f"lad_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 1e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3 (its best at this rung)", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)])),
    ("Transolver, physical velocity, lr 3e-3", fp([f"t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("Transolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
]
out = "| arm | surface pressure error, seed mean (seeds) |\n|---|---|\n"
for lab, v in arms:
    out += f"| {lab} | {mean(v):.4f} ({' / '.join(f'{x:.4f}' for x in v)}) |\n"
print(out)
g, t = ud["gt_physical_35_vs_gt_unit_35"], ud["transolver_physical_35_vs_transolver_unit_35"]
print(f": The input-scale control at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure "
      f"on the 180 shared validation cases, float32, final-epoch checkpoints, 10,000 cells (the exploration budget), 500 epochs. Paired per case, "
      f"the unit-direction GeoTransolver is lower than its physical-velocity twin on {g['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of "
      f"{g['n_cases']} cases (median factor {g['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}) and the unit-direction Transolver on "
      f"{t['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of {t['n_cases']} (median factor {t['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}). "
      f"How to read this: the physical-velocity rows measure an input scale, not an architecture; the unit-direction rows are the protocol. Data: "
      f"results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json, results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json (paired counts). {{#tbl-unit-vs-physical}}")
```
:::

Three consequences follow. Every architecture receives each global
direction as a unit vector and each magnitude as a scalar, and a comparison
against a baseline fed a raw vector is reported only as a measurement of the
input scale. The unit-direction baseline is the reference baseline on every
rung. And the input scale is fixed by rule rather than by control:
learning-rate, training-length and seed controls vary the optimizer and
cannot detect an input-scale defect. On DrivAerML, whose solver velocity is
of order tens of metres per second, and on the DrivAerML Volume task, the
trained difference between the two inputs is inside seed spread
(@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict); the rule applies on every dataset regardless,
because a rule that depends on the dataset's units is not a rule.

## The fair-comparison protocol {#sec-fair-comparison}

**Every cross-architecture number in this book is produced under the
following rules; a comparison that violates one is not reported.** The
datasets and splits are in @sec-splits, the metric in @sec-metrics and the
training recipe in @sec-protocol.

1. **Matched cells per case: 200,000 sampled surface cells for every
   architecture, the reporting protocol.** Accuracy is flat in the cell
   count above 100,000 for every model and is not below it
   (@sec-equal-budget), so a cell mismatch would be a handicap
   disguised as an architecture difference. A number at any other count
   carries its label.
2. **Matched epochs: 500 for every arm.** Doubling GeoTransolver's budget at
   the small rungs does not lower its error (@sec-data-efficiency), and at
   435 cars and 200,000 cells 1,000 epochs move neither ISLA nor
   GeoTransolver outside seed spread (@sec-nb-isocost-verdict), so 500
   under-trains neither.
3. **Each architecture at its own best learning rate, chosen by
   validation.** ISLA runs at 1e-3 at width 192 and at the width rule's
   rate above it (@sec-using-lr). GeoTransolver receives a two-rate control,
   1e-3 and 3e-3, on every rung and is reported at the better, a search
   that favors the baseline: at the reporting protocol its better rate is
   3e-3 on every DrivAerML rung and on the wings (@sec-lr-protocol).
4. **Every architecture receives each global direction as a unit vector and
   each magnitude as a scalar** (@sec-unit-direction-rule).
5. **Two or more seeds per cell, reported individually**, so the reader can
   see whether a ratio exceeds the seed spread.
6. **Shared validation cases**, sampled with the same seed, for every
   architecture.
7. **Paired per-case statistics where a ratio is claimed**: the count of
   validation cases on which one architecture is more accurate, with median
   and worst-decile per-case ratios, alongside the ratio of means.
8. **Sealed test splits evaluated once**, taken verbatim from the dataset
   manifest; sealed per checkpoint, not per program (@sec-splits).
9. **Preregistered bars**: each experiment states, in readout units and
   before it runs, the value that confirms and the value that refutes.

### One instrument per dataset {#sec-review-instrument}

**Every number in a family of comparisons is read from one fixed
instrument, and a control that changes the instrument is reported as a
control.** The *instrument* for a dataset is its fixed validation set and
evaluation configuration: on the DrivAerML Surface task, surface pressure
and wall shear on 48 held-out cars at 200,000 sampled cells, scored in
float32; on the DrivAerML Volume task, pressure, velocity and turbulent
viscosity at the interior queries of the same 48 cars; on HiLiftAeroML,
pressure, velocity and wall shear on 180 held-out cases shared by every
training split, at the same count and precision; on AirfRANS, pressure,
velocity and turbulent viscosity at the interior queries of its 200 test
airfoils. An instrument is never widened after a result is read from it; a
control that changes it (another cell count, a rotated pose, a biased
sampling density) is reported as such and never mixed into an in-family
number. Its limits bind where stated: 48 cars is a small validation set and
two seeds a thin noise estimate (@sec-limits).

## Resource matching {#sec-resource-matching}

**Every cross-architecture comparison states, on both sides, the parameter
count, the cells per case and the training memory, or says in the same
sentence where they differ and whether the difference could buy accuracy.**
The parity row of the DrivAerML Surface task is matched on parameters and
on cells per case; the footprints of both sides are read from the protocol
lanes' own training logs in @tbl-isla-cost. Memory is not a controlled
variable in any comparison and no accuracy result depends on it: the
checkpoints in this book are trained by implementations of the same
function that differ only in footprint. Where the two architectures are
compared at unequal parameters or memory, the section that does so says
which side has more and whether it bought accuracy (@sec-equal-budget).

### Configuration of the evidence lanes {#sec-evidence-lane-config}

**The evidence lanes of the surface tasks carry ISLA at width 192 with the
linear routing form; the reference configuration (@sec-using-config)
re-measures them, and where a reference-configuration artifact exists it is
the row.** This paragraph is the one place the book states it; individual
tables and captions name their lane's width and rate and do not narrate the
difference. Lanes that already carry the reference form are the 35-wing rung
of HiLiftAeroML at 200,000 cells, the DrivAerML Volume task at 1e-3, the
384-wide, 24-layer DrivAerML Surface lane at 200,000 cells, and every
AirfRANS lane. @sec-program-status lists which lanes remain.

## Learning rate {#sec-lr-protocol}

**Each architecture trains at its own best learning rate, and the rate is
part of the protocol, not a tuning afterthought.** GeoTransolver's best rate
at the reporting protocol is 3e-3 on every DrivAerML rung and on the wings,
found by the two-rate control of rule 3; Transolver runs at 3e-3; ISLA runs
at 1e-3 at width 192 and at the width rule's starting rate above it
(@sec-using-lr). Why ISLA's rate does not simply follow the baselines' is a
property of the routing form and is explained once, in
@sec-isla-routing-forms.

## Datasets {#sec-datasets}

**Three datasets are training and evaluation sources, and a fourth is a
zero-shot target.** All four supply the same input schema, boundary cells
with positions, outward normals and measures plus the global conditions, so
one model implementation runs on all of them. Every one is an instance of
external aerodynamics with $K = 1$ global direction, the far-field flow
direction, and $S \in \{0, 1\}$ global scalars.

| dataset | what it is | what varies | global inputs | role in the book |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DrivAerML** (cars) | 484 parametrically morphed DrivAer notchback variants; time-averaged surface pressure and wall shear on about 8.8 million surface cells per car, plus volume fields | geometry only; one far-field condition | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | the Surface task: full-data accuracy, discretization and pose probes, capacity ladders; the Volume task: boundary to interior |
| **HiLiftAeroML** (wings) | 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing geometries (flap and slat settings by Latin hypercube), each at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°; surface pressure, velocity and wall shear | geometry and far-field direction | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | data efficiency, unseen geometry, regime extrapolation |
| **AirfRANS** (airfoils) | 1,001 two-dimensional incompressible RANS solutions around NACA airfoils; pressure, velocity and turbulent viscosity in the volume | geometry, inlet direction and inlet speed | $K = 1$, $S = 1$ | the interior task on a second dataset; the training-case axis |
| **SHIFT-SUV** | sport-utility bodies in two rear-end families, estate and fastback; surface pressure and wall shear; same reference length and far-field direction as DrivAerML at a lower speed | geometry; a speed shift common to every architecture | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | zero-shot transfer target only |

### DrivAerML: the Surface task and the Volume task {#sec-benchmarks}

**DrivAerML carries two tasks, named separately throughout the book because
they measure different things.** Geometry is the only variable, there is
one far-field condition, and every model is fed the vehicle surface alone:
the information diet of every published baseline on the dataset. The recipe
assigns 435 variants to training and 48 to validation; the remaining variant
is in neither. The reporting protocol samples the recipe's default of
200,000 surface cells per case per step. The **DrivAerML Surface task**
predicts pressure and wall shear at those cells (@sec-surface). The
**DrivAerML Volume task** predicts pressure, velocity and turbulent
viscosity at 200,000 interior query points per car from the surface alone
(@sec-interior). A sentence that compares architectures on DrivAerML names
one of the two.

### HiLiftAeroML

**HiLiftAeroML is a full geometry-by-angle grid, so it can hold out each
axis of variation on its own.** Every geometry appears at every angle, and
the dataset supports splits along three independent directions: how many
cases, which angles, and which geometries. It is one of the two datasets on
which the data-efficiency ladder is measured (@sec-data-efficiency); the
other is the DrivAerML Surface task.

### AirfRANS {#sec-dataset-airfrans}

**AirfRANS is the interior task on a second dataset and a second PDE
regime, and the first instance in the book of a global scalar input.** Its
full split trains on 800 airfoils and tests on 200. The boundary is the
airfoil polyline, about a thousand segments with in-plane normals and
segment lengths as the quadrature measure; the global inputs are the inlet
direction as the one global vector and the inlet speed as the one global
scalar; the interior queries carry the signed distance to the airfoil.
Pressure is nondimensionalized by the inlet dynamic pressure and velocity
by the inlet speed; turbulent viscosity keeps its units and the recipe's
normalization. The interior results are in @sec-interior-airfrans.

### SHIFT-SUV {#sec-shift-suv}

**No main result trains on SHIFT-SUV; its fastback family is the zero-shot
target.** Its curated manifest separates the estate family (794 / 99 / 100
cases for training / validation / test) from the fastback family
(796 / 99 / 99). The fastback family is held out from every model in the
book and is the zero-shot target of the cross-family transfer measurements
(@sec-scoreboard-200k); the estate training split is a training source only where
a two-family model is compared. Its lower far-field speed is a covariate
shift identical for every architecture, none of which receives the Reynolds
number, and it is reported alongside the geometry-family shift rather than
corrected.

### Datasets beyond external aerodynamics {#sec-datasets-beyond-aero}

**The architecture is written for any steady boundary-driven PDE, and
external aerodynamics is its benchmark instance, not its scope.** The next
benchmark instances are steady problems whose boundary conditions and loads
vary per sample, which exercise the global vector and scalar inputs and the
per-cell boundary scalars that the aerodynamic datasets leave at $K = 1$
and $n_b = 0$: PLAID Tensile2d (two-dimensional solid mechanics under a
varying load with material parameters as global scalars, labeled boundary
edges, and the laboratory frame as two global vectors because its targets
are stress components in that frame, @sec-isla-heads), GINOT Bracket Lug (three-dimensional elastoplasticity under
a varying pressure load, with published Transolver and GNOT numbers), and
GNOT Heat2d (steady conduction with a prescribed temperature function on a
labeled edge, the $K = 0$ case with per-cell boundary scalars). Within
aerodynamics, AeroZoo is the in-generation diversity benchmark: a dataset of
dissimilar bodies built to stress generalization across geometry families
rather than within one. None of these carries a number in this book; the
open axis they represent is stated in @sec-limits.

### Splits {#sec-splits}

**Each HiLiftAeroML split holds out one question, and the splits are the
dataset's curated manifests, used unchanged.** @tbl-hilift-splits lists
them. The *data-efficiency* family is nested (@fig-hilift-splits): 35
training cases $\subset$ 210 $\subset$ 510 $\subset$ 1,260, all scored on
one shared 180-case validation set (180 cases on 118 geometries), with a
360-case test set that no data-efficiency experiment touches. Because the
rungs are subsets of the same 1,260 cases, a validation geometry may appear
in training at other angles: these rungs measure sample complexity, not
unseen geometry. The two *regime-extrapolation* splits hold out flow
physics, with stall onset determined per geometry from the lift curve. The
*geometry* family holds out geometries at all ten angles. The three
*fixed-angle* splits remove the direction dependence entirely and so control
for whether an advantage comes from representing the far-field direction.

| family | split | train | val | test | what it holds out |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| data efficiency | nested rungs | 35, 210, 510, 1,260 | 180 | 360 | nothing; measures sample complexity (validation geometries may recur in training at other angles) |
| regime extrapolation | angle of attack | 788 (angles up to 12°) | 112 | 900 (14° and above) | higher angles of attack |
| regime extrapolation | stall | 942 (pre-stall) | 135 | 723 (post-stall) | post-stall flow |
| unseen geometry | geometry | 1,260, 210 or 40 cases (126, 21 or 4 geometries) | 18 geometries, all ten angles | 36 geometries, all ten angles | the geometry itself |
| fixed angle | 4°, 12°, 22° | 126 geometries at one angle | 18 geometries at that angle | — | the far-field direction as a variable |

: The HiLiftAeroML splits, in cases unless a cell says geometries. Every
split is a curated manifest of the dataset revision named in the warning
below; the fixed-angle splits have no test set. How to read this: a row is
one question; the manifests overlap (see the warning), so the test columns
are held out per checkpoint, not per program. {#tbl-hilift-splits}

```{python}
#| label: fig-hilift-splits
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The HiLiftAeroML data-efficiency family, to scale. The bar is the
#|   1,800-case grid; the nested training rungs (35, 210, 510, 1,260 cases)
#|   are subsets of one another, all scored on the same 180 validation
#|   cases, and the 360-case test set is sealed. How to read this: widths
#|   are case counts; the bar does not show which angles or geometries fall
#|   in each rung, and the regime, geometry and fixed-angle families are
#|   separate manifests not drawn here.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.0, 1.9))
shades = ["#1f5aa3", BLUE, BLUE_LIGHT, BLUE_PALE]
for n, col in zip([1260, 510, 210, 35], shades):
    ax.barh(0, n, left=0, height=0.6, color=col, edgecolor="white", lw=0.8)
ax.barh(0, 180, left=1260, height=0.6, color=BASELINE, edgecolor="white", lw=0.8)
ax.barh(0, 360, left=1440, height=0.6, color=PAPER, edgecolor=BASELINE, lw=0.8, hatch="///")
for x, label in [(35 / 2, "35"), (35 + 175 / 2, "210"), (210 + 300 / 2, "510"),
                 (510 + 750 / 2, "1,260 training cases (nested rungs)")]:
    ax.text(x, 0, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color="white" if x > 200 else INK)
ax.text(1260 + 90, 0, "val\n180", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK)
ax.text(1440 + 180, 0, "sealed test 360", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1800); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 0.6); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xticks([0, 35, 210, 510, 1260, 1440, 1800])
ax.set_xticklabels(["0", "35", "210", "510", "1,260", "1,440", "1,800"], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("cases [count]")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**DrivAerML has one validation set of 48 cars, fixed across every
experiment and shared by the Surface and Volume tasks.** The training set
is 435 cars, or a nested rung of 27, 54, 109 or 218 cars for the
data-efficiency ladder (@sec-data-efficiency). Sampling-density and pose
probes evaluate the same 48 cars with transformed inputs
(@sec-discretization-centerpiece). AirfRANS uses its full split's 800
training and 200 test airfoils, with nested rungs of 50, 100, 200 and 400
airfoils for its training-case axis (@sec-compute-allocation).

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="The HiLiftAeroML manifests overlap, so a test split is sealed per checkpoint, not per program"}
The manifests are separate but not disjoint. The angle-of-attack and stall
test sets between them contain every one of the 180 geometries, and the
360-case data-efficiency test set shares 179 cases with them, the geometry
test set 182 and the deflection test set 182 (37 and 40 of their cases also
sit in the shared validation set). A test split is therefore *held out per
checkpoint*, since no model evaluated on it trained on it; but once the
regime-extrapolation tests are read, no HiLiftAeroML geometry remains
unexposed at the level of the program, and no later evaluation on these
manifests is an independent program-level confirmation
(@sec-limits-validation). The dataset revision used throughout is
`bbec30bcfc6103309c1375c5228b3ad0a586bfaf`, in which six cases' force
coefficients are surface-field integrations rather than solver monitor
means; the book's force errors never use the dataset's coefficients as
reference.
:::

## Protocol {#sec-protocol}

**One frozen recipe produces every cross-architecture number in the book;
a comparison that departs from it says so in the same sentence.**

| item | setting |
|---|---|
| cells per case | 200,000 sampled surface cells per case per step, the recipe default and the reporting protocol, every architecture and every dataset; on the interior tasks, 200,000 interior queries per case on DrivAerML and 100,000 on AirfRANS |
| exploration budget | 10,000 cells per case: appears only as a labeled rung of a cell-count ladder or as the labeled setting of a mechanism control, never as an accuracy standing |
| epochs and schedule | 500 epochs, one case per step; the learning rate is divided by ten every 100 epochs, so the effective budget is about 300 epochs at a useful rate |
| arithmetic | bfloat16 autocast in training; float32 at evaluation (@sec-metrics) |
| augmentation | none |
| learning rate | each architecture at its own best rate at the reporting protocol: ISLA $10^{-3}$ at width 192 and the width rule's rate above it (@sec-using-lr), GeoTransolver and Transolver $3 \times 10^{-3}$; every row names the rate it uses (@sec-lr-protocol) |
| global inputs | each global direction as a unit vector, each magnitude as a scalar, for every architecture (@sec-unit-direction-rule) |
| seeds | two or more (42 and 43 unless stated), reported individually beside the mean |
| checkpoint | the final epoch; no selection on validation error |
| datasets | a result counts when it is reproduced on two datasets; a single-dataset result is labeled as such |
| validation and test | all architectures at all rungs scored on the same validation cases; a sealed test split is evaluated exactly once with the checkpoint and configuration declared in writing beforehand |
| preregistration | every experiment states its prediction and its falsifier in readout units before it runs; the dated record is the notebook (@sec-notebook) |

Because the rungs of a ladder share one rate and one schedule, a difference
between rungs is a difference in data and nothing else. When a result
favors one architecture, the strongest controls for the other (a higher
learning rate, doubled epochs, a same-family architecture without the
geometry encoder) run under the same recipe before the result is stated.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="What the validation set is used for"}
The HiLiftAeroML and DrivAerML accuracy figures in this book are
validation-set figures with no checkpoint selection behind them, and with
this much adaptive reuse disclosed: the per-architecture learning rate is
chosen on the full split by validation; Transolver's rate is chosen per
small-data rung on it; the ablations that follow earlier readouts are
designed after reading it; and the choice of which results to present is
made with it in view. The HiLiftAeroML test splits are spent only on the
regime-extrapolation evaluations and one diagnostic run alongside them (a
variant of ISLA given raw coordinates), and because those test sets cover
every geometry (@sec-splits), the remaining test manifests are held out per
checkpoint but are not program-level confirmations (@sec-limits-validation).
:::

Every figure and table caption ends with the artifact in `results/` from
which it is computed, and every figure is drawn from that artifact at render
time.
